source: Extracted from CURRICULUM.html's unit cards on 2026-10-27. The page is the agreed syllabus; if the two disagree, the page wins and this file is regenerated.

parts.name: Part A — a finite quantum system, mathematics first
parts.headline: Five units that turn four experiments into a definition, and prove the definition is the only one that works
parts.thesis: Stern–Gerlach forces complex amplitudes, the Mach–Zehnder interferometer forces relative phase, the precessing spin forces unitary evolution, and two photons from one crystal force the tensor product. Part A ends with the density operator, the object that says what a subsystem knows when it is entangled with something you cannot see. Five units, 37 h.

parts.name: Part B — correlations: what entanglement can and cannot do
parts.headline: Entanglement is stronger than any classical correlation and still cannot send a message, and both halves are theorems
parts.thesis: No-cloning and imperfect distinguishability say what a single unknown state withholds; Bell and Tsirelson bound what shared entanglement gives, from both sides; teleportation and dense coding spend it as a resource with exact exchange rates. Two branches take it further — into information theory and into cryptography. Five units, 35 h.

parts.name: Part C — circuits, and the complexity class they define
parts.headline: A quantum computer is a uniform family of circuits, and three units are enough to say exactly what that buys
parts.thesis: Exact universality first, because it is pure linear algebra; then approximate universality, which is where the cost of finite gate sets is paid and where the T gate becomes special; then BQP, placed between BPP and PP with every inclusion proved. Three units, 23 h.

parts.name: Part D — algorithms: interference as a resource, and its limits
parts.headline: Every speedup here is structure exploited by interference, and the last spine unit proves that without structure there is almost nothing to exploit
parts.thesis: The query model, because it is where separations can be proved; Simon's problem as the first honest exponential separation; the Fourier transform over finite groups as the engine; Shor as its payoff; Grover as the unstructured counterpart; and the lower bounds that say Grover is the best possible. Hamiltonian simulation returns to Feynman's original reason for the whole enterprise, and a branch, QMA, proves the quantum Cook–Levin theorem and finds the problem even a quantum computer cannot solve. Eight units, 60 h.

parts.name: Part E — noise, error correction, and the honest state of the art
parts.headline: Every obstacle to quantum error correction looks fundamental, and each one is removed by a theorem
parts.thesis: Noise as completely positive maps; codes that correct continuous errors by correcting four discrete ones; the stabiliser formalism, which makes codes computable and makes Clifford circuits classically simulable; and the threshold theorem, which turns all of it into arithmetic about physical error rates. Two branches come down to the device: one derives how a real qubit is driven and why it leaks, the other asks what hardware exists and what it has actually shown. Six units, 47.5 h.

units.title: Why complex numbers: unbiased bases, and the spectral theorem for normal operators
units.theory: The Stern–Gerlach experiment as a puzzle with no theory attached: silver atoms through an inhomogeneous field split into exactly two beams; filter one, measure along a perpendicular axis, and the split is 50/50; measure along the original axis again and the first result is gone. Take the minimal model — states are unit vectors, outcome probabilities are |⟨u, v⟩|² — and ask whether it fits in ℝ². It does not: the three spatial axes give three pairwise mutually unbiased bases, and ℝ² has room for two.
units.tools: Complex inner-product spaces, sesquilinearity, the adjoint. Dirac notation as notation for the Riesz isomorphism V → V*: a bra is a dual vector, nothing more, and |u⟩⟨v| is a rank-one map. Hermitian, unitary and normal operators. Schur triangularisation, then the spectral theorem for normal operators proved from it; simultaneous diagonalisation of commuting normal operators. Functional calculus: f(A) for normal A, and e^iH unitary for Hermitian H.
units.problems: The slides prove that ℝ² admits at most two mutually unbiased bases — every unit vector unbiased to the standard basis lies at ±45°, and there is only one such basis — and exhibit three in ℂ² (the eigenbases of what unit 02 will call σ_z, σ_x, σ_y). That three is the maximum in ℂ² is left as a debt for unit 02. The sheet computes e^iθσ_x = cos θ · I + i sin θ · σ_x three ways (series, spectral, Cayley–Hamilton), shows a non-normal matrix with no orthonormal eigenbasis, proves that unitaries preserve unbiasedness, and states (cited: Wootters–Fields 1989) that ℂ^d holds d + 1 mutually unbiased bases when d is a prime power.
units.checkpoint: You prove the spectral theorem for normal operators from Schur, and prove that ℝ² holds at most two mutually unbiased bases while ℂ² holds at least three — so that “amplitudes are complex” is, for you, a theorem about an experiment.

units.title: The postulates, as mathematics: states, measurement, and evolution
units.theory: The running example is the Mach–Zehnder interferometer: one photon, two beam splitters, a phase shifter in one arm, and a detector that never clicks when the arms are balanced. Probabilities cannot add here; amplitudes do. From it, the postulates: a state is a ray in a complex Hilbert space (unit vector modulo global phase, and why the global phase is unobservable while the relative one runs the interferometer); an observable is a self-adjoint operator; the Born rule and projective measurement with its post-measurement state; and closed-system evolution is unitary.
units.tools: Spectral projections and the Born rule as a probability measure on the spectrum; expectation and variance as ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ and its square. Stone's theorem in finite dimension, proved: every continuous one-parameter group of unitaries is e^−iHt for a unique Hermitian H — so the Schrödinger equation is not a separate postulate but the generator of the evolution postulate. The Robertson uncertainty relation ΔA ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A, B]⟩| from Cauchy–Schwarz, and why it is a statement about preparations, not about disturbance.
units.problems: The slides compute the Mach–Zehnder detector probabilities as cos²(φ/2) and sin²(φ/2), and then insert a which-path detector and watch the fringes vanish. The sheet works the Elitzur–Vaidman bomb tester — a live bomb certified without being touched — to its single-pass numbers, then shows that a chain of N weakly-coupled stages pushes the certification probability to 1 − O(1/N), which is the quantum Zeno effect arriving as an exercise. Also: prove two states differing by a global phase give identical statistics for every observable, and that a relative phase does not.
units.checkpoint: For the Elitzur–Vaidman setup with a live bomb you derive the three outcome probabilities — ½ explodes, ¼ certified untouched, ¼ inconclusive — and you prove finite-dimensional Stone's theorem.

units.title: One qubit: the Bloch sphere, and the group that rotates it twice
units.theory: A spin in a magnetic field precesses, and the precession is the whole of single-qubit dynamics. The pure states of a qubit are ℂP¹, which is a sphere: the Bloch map, proved a bijection onto S², with orthogonal states at antipodes. Pauli matrices, the Pauli vector, and e^−iθ n·σ/2 as rotation by θ about n. Larmor precession and Rabi oscillation as the two pictures every hardware platform is controlled with; the rotating-wave approximation stated with its condition.
units.tools: SU(2) and SO(3); the homomorphism SU(2) → SO(3) via conjugation of the Pauli vector, proved surjective with kernel {±I}. Consequently a 2π rotation multiplies a spinor by −1, which is observable in interference with an unrotated reference (neutron interferometry, 1975, cited). Every single-qubit unitary is e^iαR_z(β)R_y(γ)R_z(δ), proved.
units.problems: The slides run a proton in an MRI magnet as the example: gyromagnetic ratio γ/2π = 42.58 MHz/T, so 63.87 MHz at 1.5 T. The sheet pays unit 00's debt — two bases of ℂ² are mutually unbiased if and only if their Bloch axes are orthogonal, so ℂ² holds exactly three — finds the axis and angle of given 2 × 2 unitaries, produces ZYZ angles, and designs a π-pulse of given Rabi frequency.
units.checkpoint: Given any 2 × 2 unitary you produce its rotation axis and angle on the Bloch sphere and its ZYZ decomposition, and you prove SU(2) → SO(3) is surjective with kernel {±I}.

units.title: Two systems: the tensor product, and the states that are not products
units.theory: A nonlinear crystal turns one photon into two whose polarisations, measured in the same basis, always disagree — in every basis — a fact no assignment of separate states to each photon reproduces. The composite-system postulate: the joint space is H_A ⊗ H_B, not H_A ⊕ H_B, and the difference is the difference between 2n and 2^n dimensions for n qubits. Product and entangled states; the four Bell states; measuring one subsystem as the projective measurement P ⊗ I.
units.tools: The tensor product defined by its universal property — the bilinear map V × W → V ⊗ W through which every bilinear map factors uniquely — then constructed, with uniqueness up to unique isomorphism proved. Bases and dimension; A ⊗ B on operators and the Kronecker matrix. The Schmidt decomposition, proved from the singular value decomposition, and Schmidt rank as the criterion: a pure bipartite state is entangled if and only if its rank exceeds one.
units.problems: The slides show the dimension count that makes the subject: product states of n qubits form a 2n-real-parameter family inside a space of 2^n+1 − 2. The sheet: a two-qubit state is entangled exactly when the determinant of its 2 × 2 coefficient matrix is non-zero; Schmidt-decompose given states; prove |Φ⁺⟩ is invariant under U ⊗ Ū for every unitary U, which is the algebraic heart of unit 07.
units.checkpoint: You prove the universal property determines V ⊗ W up to unique isomorphism, and for any two-qubit state you decide entanglement and compute the Schmidt coefficients.

units.title: Density operators: what a subsystem knows, and why Alice cannot signal
units.theory: Half of a Bell pair is not in any pure state, so the state space must grow. Density operators: positive, trace one, convex; pure if and only if tr ρ² = 1. For a qubit, the Bloch ball, with the maximally mixed state at the centre. Two different preparation stories — |0⟩ or |1⟩ with probability ½, and |+⟩ or |−⟩ with probability ½ — give the same operator and therefore identical statistics for every measurement: the operator is the state, the story is not.
units.tools: The partial trace, defined as the unique linear map with tr((A ⊗ I)ρ) = tr(A ρ_A) for all A, and uniqueness proved. Purification, proved to exist. The Schrödinger–HJW theorem: two ensembles give the same density operator if and only if they are related by an isometry, proved. The no-signalling theorem: nothing Alice does locally — unitary or measurement — changes ρ_B, proved in two lines from the definition of partial trace.
units.problems: The slides take the partial trace of each Bell state and get I/2 every time. The sheet: purify a given qubit state; find the unitary relating two given ensembles; show a pure bipartite state is entangled if and only if its reduced state is mixed; prove the Bloch ball is exactly the set of 2 × 2 density operators.
units.checkpoint: You prove the no-signalling theorem from the defining property of the partial trace, and exhibit the HJW isometry between two given ensembles for the maximally mixed qubit.

units.title: No-cloning, and how well two states can be told apart
units.theory: Opened by history, because here the history is the argument: Herbert's 1982 FLASH proposal for faster-than-light signalling, which needed a copier, and the two papers that killed it within months. The no-cloning theorem proved twice — once from linearity, once from preservation of inner products, where ⟨ψ|φ⟩ = ⟨ψ|φ⟩² forces 0 or 1. Orthogonal states copy freely (CNOT is a classical copier), so the theorem is precisely about non-orthogonality.
units.tools: Non-orthogonal states cannot be perfectly distinguished, proved. The Helstrom bound for two equiprobable pure states, ½(1 + √(1 − |⟨ψ|φ⟩|²)), proved by reducing to the plane the two states span. The optimal universal cloner's fidelity 5/6 stated (Bužek–Hillery, cited). Unambiguous discrimination stated here and proved in unit 21, when POVMs exist.
units.problems: The slides distinguish |0⟩ from |+⟩: overlap 1/√2, optimal success ½(1 + 1/√2) = 0.8536, measuring in the basis halfway between them. The sheet: show that a perfect cloner would let Alice signal through a shared Bell pair, completing the FLASH refutation from unit 04's theorem; prove no-deleting; compute Helstrom for states at Bloch angle θ.
units.checkpoint: You prove no-cloning both ways and prove the Helstrom bound, producing 0.8536 and the optimal measurement for |0⟩ versus |+⟩.

units.title: Bell, CHSH and Tsirelson: the classical bound, the quantum bound, and the gap between
units.theory: A local hidden-variable model defined as mathematics — a probability space Λ and response functions for each party depending only on their own setting — so that “local realism” is a hypothesis with content. The CHSH quantity, bounded by 2 in every such model, proved. The singlet with the right four angles reaches 2√2. The experiments: Aspect 1982; the 2015 loophole-free tests, Delft's at S = 2.42 ± 0.20 over 1.3 km; the 2022 Nobel prize.
units.tools: Tsirelson's bound, proved: for ±1-valued observables C² = 4I − [A, A′][B, B′], so ‖C‖ ≤ 2√2. The CHSH game as a nonlocal game: 3/4 classically, cos²(π/8) quantumly. The Popescu–Rohrlich box reaches 4 while respecting no-signalling — so no-signalling is not what stops quantum mechanics at 2√2, and why it stops there remains a live question.
units.problems: The slides derive the optimal angles and the value 2√2 from the singlet's correlation −cos(θ_a − θ_b). The sheet: prove the classical bound by reducing to deterministic strategies; show the PR box is no-signalling; prove the CHSH game value cos²(π/8) ≈ 0.854 is optimal; and read Delft's S = 2.42 ± 0.20 critically — how many standard deviations above 2, and why the authors reported a p-value of 0.039 rather than a sigma count.
units.checkpoint: You prove CHSH ≤ 2 for every local hidden-variable model and ≤ 2√2 for every quantum strategy, and produce measurement directions on the singlet that attain 2√2.

units.title: Teleportation and dense coding: the exchange rate between qubits, bits and ebits
units.theory: Teleportation derived as one algebraic identity: |ψ⟩ ⊗ |Φ⁺⟩ rewritten in the Bell basis on Alice's side. One ebit and two classical bits move one qubit; the original is destroyed, so no-cloning survives; and before the bits arrive Bob holds I/2, so no-signalling survives. Superdense coding runs the trade the other way. Entanglement swapping as teleportation of half a pair. Experiments: Innsbruck 1997; Micius 2017, ground to satellite.
units.tools: Resource inequalities as bookkeeping: 1 ebit + 2 cbits ≥ 1 qubit; 1 ebit + 1 qubit ≥ 2 cbits. The Holevo bound stated (cited here, proved in branch 08): one qubit alone never carries more than one bit, so dense coding is optimal. Average fidelity over the Bloch sphere as the figure of merit, and the classical measure-and-prepare benchmark of 2/3.
units.problems: The slides draw the teleportation circuit and trace all four branches. The sheet: show the naive measure-in-Z-and-resend strategy has average fidelity 1 − ½⟨sin²θ⟩ = 2/3, and state (cited, Massar–Popescu 1995) that no classical strategy does better — so a measured fidelity above 2/3 certifies that something quantum happened; verify entanglement swapping; teleport through a noisy pair and compute the fidelity as a function of the noise.
units.checkpoint: You derive teleportation with all four corrections, prove Bob's state is I/2 until the bits arrive, and compute the 2/3 classical benchmark.

units.title: Entropy and the Holevo bound: how many bits a qubit holds
units.theory: A qubit has a continuum of states and yields one bit. Shannon entropy as the answer to “how many bits” for a classical source; von Neumann entropy as its quantum successor, equal to the Shannon entropy of the spectrum. Concavity, subadditivity, the Araki–Lieb inequality, proved; strong subadditivity stated (Lieb–Ruskai 1973, cited) and used. The Holevo bound on accessible information, proved from strong subadditivity in the form that discarding a subsystem never increases quantum mutual information — the case of the monotonicity of relative entropy that strong subadditivity is.
units.tools: Relative entropy and Klein's inequality, proved. Typical sequences and typical subspaces; Schumacher compression stated with its rate S(ρ) and the proof's structure given. Entanglement entropy of a pure bipartite state as the unique measure of pure-state entanglement (stated).
units.problems: The sheet: compute the Holevo quantity for |0⟩ and |+⟩ sent with equal probability — the average state has eigenvalues cos²(π/8) and sin²(π/8), so χ = 0.601 bits, against one bit for orthogonal states; prove superdense coding saturates Holevo with an ebit; show that the whole can have less entropy than a part, S(AB) < S(A), for an entangled state and never for a separable one.
units.checkpoint: You prove the Holevo bound from strong subadditivity and compute χ = 0.601 bits for the |0⟩/|+⟩ ensemble.

units.title: Quantum key distribution: disturbance as a security guarantee
units.theory: No-cloning turned from a limitation into a weapon. BB84: random bases, sifting, error estimation, then classical error correction and privacy amplification, each step's job named. E91: the same key from a Bell pair, with a CHSH test as the eavesdropper alarm — the seed of device-independent cryptography, where security rests on unit 06's inequality rather than on trusting the hardware. Micius 2017, satellite-to-ground over 1200 km.
units.tools: The information–disturbance trade-off for BB84 states, proved for intercept-resend. The Shor–Preskill key rate 1 − 2h(Q) for quantum bit error rate Q, stated with its proof cited, and its reading: error correction costs h(Q), privacy amplification costs another. What QKD does not do: authenticate, which still needs a shared secret.
units.problems: The sheet: show intercept-resend in a random basis yields a 25 per cent error rate on the sifted key; compute the key rate at Q = 5 per cent (0.427 bits per sifted bit); find where it reaches zero (Q ≈ 11.0 per cent); show that a CHSH value of 2√2 leaves an eavesdropper no information in E91.
units.checkpoint: You prove intercept-resend causes 25 per cent error, and produce the 11.0 per cent threshold from the Shor–Preskill rate.

units.title: Circuits: reversible classical computation, and exact universality
units.theory: The circuit model: qubits as wires, gates as unitaries on few of them, measurement at the end. The principle of deferred measurement, proved, so that end-only measurement loses nothing. Classical computation inside it: Toffoli is universal for reversible computation, and Bennett's uncomputation removes the garbage, proved — so every polynomial-time f yields a polynomial circuit |x⟩|y⟩ ↦ |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩, which is what every oracle in Part D is.
units.tools: Every unitary on ℂ^d is a product of two-level unitaries, proved; Gray codes move each onto adjacent basis states; so CNOT plus single-qubit gates is exactly universal, proved (Barenco et al. 1995). Controlled-U from single-qubit gates and two CNOTs via the ZYZ form of unit 02. The counting lower bound: a generic n-qubit unitary has 4^n − 1 real parameters, so exact synthesis needs Ω(4^n) gates — most unitaries are not efficiently implementable, and the interesting ones are the exceptions.
units.problems: The slides build Toffoli from six CNOTs, two Hadamards and seven T or T† gates, and verify it on all eight inputs. The sheet: build controlled-controlled-U; compile a given two-qubit unitary; prove deferred measurement; uncompute a garbage register for a reversible adder. Optionally, write your own statevector simulator — the tensor trick is ten lines — and test it against qclib on random circuits.
units.checkpoint: You prove CNOT plus single-qubit gates exactly universal, and build and verify the seven-T Toffoli circuit.

units.title: Finite gate sets: density, Solovay–Kitaev, and why the T gate is the expensive one
units.theory: A real machine has finitely many gates, so universality must be approximate. Operator-norm distance, and errors add along a circuit: ‖U_n⋯U₁ − V_n⋯V₁‖ ≤ Σ‖U_i − V_i‖, proved. {H, T} generates a dense subgroup of SU(2) up to phase: T · HTH is a rotation by an angle θ with cos(θ/2) = cos²(π/8), an irrational multiple of π — density proved, the irrationality too, in four lines of algebraic integers. The Clifford group as the normaliser of the Pauli group; Clifford + T as the standard universal set.
units.tools: The Solovay–Kitaev theorem: any gate to accuracy ε in O(log^c(1/ε)) gates, c ≈ 4 in the Dawson–Nielsen version, with the balanced group-commutator step proved and the recursion's analysis cited. Exact synthesis over Clifford + T (Kliuchnikov–Maslov–Mosca: entries in ℤ[1/√2, i]) and optimal z-rotations at about 3 log₂(1/ε) T gates (Ross–Selinger), both cited — the number fault tolerance will later charge for.
units.problems: The sheet: given a circuit of 10⁹ gates and a 1 per cent total error budget, find the per-gate accuracy (10⁻¹¹) and the T-count of each arbitrary rotation (about 110); show Clifford gates map Paulis to Paulis; prove the subadditivity bound is tight up to constants.
units.checkpoint: You prove the error-accumulation bound and the density of ⟨H, T⟩, and carry a whole-circuit error budget down to a per-rotation T-count.

units.title: BQP, and where it sits among the classes you already know
units.theory: BQP defined with uniform circuit families and error ⅓; independence of the gate set, by unit 11. Amplification by majority vote, proved with Hoeffding. Then the placement: BPP ⊆ BQP (coins from Hadamards, reversibility from unit 10), BQP ⊆ PSPACE (Feynman's sum over paths, evaluated depth-first in polynomial space), and BQP ⊆ PP (Adleman–DeMarrais–Huang 1997: acceptance probability as a difference of two #P functions), all proved. BQP is low for itself, stated. Its Merlin–Arthur analogue, QMA, is branch 20.
units.tools: Path sums and GapP functions; restricting to gates with rational or dyadic entries without loss. What is not known: BQP versus NP in either direction. What is known relative to oracles: BQP ⊄ PH for some oracle (Raz–Tal 2018, cited), and unit 18's lower bound gives an oracle with NP ⊄ BQP. The honest summary: quantum computing is a hypothesis about BQP ≠ BPP, and no proof of it is in sight, since it would separate P from PSPACE.
units.problems: The sheet: how many repetitions push error from ⅓ to 2^−100 (about 1250 by Hoeffding); prove BQP closed under complement; show that postselected quantum computation contains NP, as the first step toward Aaronson's PostBQP = PP (cited).
units.checkpoint: You prove BQP ⊆ PP, and explain in one paragraph why a proof that BQP ≠ BPP would also prove P ≠ PSPACE.

units.title: The query model, phase kickback, and the first separations
units.theory: Oracles as unit 10's reversible circuits, counted by queries because query complexity admits lower bounds and gate complexity does not. Phase kickback, proved: querying on |−⟩ writes f(x) into a phase. Deutsch: one query against two. Deutsch–Jozsa: one query against 2^n−1 + 1 deterministic — and against a constant number of randomised queries, which is why this is not yet a separation worth having. Bernstein–Vazirani: one query against n, even for randomised algorithms.
units.tools: The Hadamard transform H^⊗n as the Fourier transform over ℤ₂^n, written via characters (−1)^x·y — the first appearance of the structure unit 15 generalises. Adversary-free classical lower bounds by counting information.
units.problems: The slides draw interference in Deutsch–Jozsa as amplitudes cancelling on the all-zero outcome. The sheet: prove the deterministic lower bound 2^n−1 + 1; show a k-query randomised test errs with probability at most 2^1−k; prove Bernstein–Vazirani's classical lower bound of n.
units.checkpoint: You prove Deutsch–Jozsa and Bernstein–Vazirani correct, and say precisely which classical model each one beats and which it does not.

units.title: Simon's problem: the first exponential separation, and the algorithm Shor read
units.theory: A function on n bits that is two-to-one with a hidden XOR-period s. Quantumly: each run yields a uniformly random y with y · s = 0, and O(n) runs plus Gaussian elimination over 𝔽₂ recover s. Classically: any randomised algorithm needs Ω(2^n/2) queries, proved by a collision argument. Relative to this oracle, BPP ≠ BQP. Simon's 1994 paper was the one Shor read, and the history is the argument: replace ℤ₂^n by ℤ_N and you are most of the way to factoring.
units.tools: Linear algebra over 𝔽₂: orthogonal complements, rank, elimination. The probability that n − 1 uniform vectors span an (n−1)-dimensional space, bounded below by ∏(1 − 2^−k) ≈ 0.289, proved; expected number of runs below n + 1.
units.problems: The sheet: run Simon by hand on n = 3 for a given s; prove the collision lower bound; show the infinite product converges to 0.2888.
units.checkpoint: You prove the quantum upper bound O(n) and the classical randomised lower bound Ω(2^n/2), and compute 0.2888.

units.title: Fourier on finite abelian groups, the quantum Fourier transform, and phase estimation
units.theory: Characters of a finite abelian group, their orthogonality, and the Fourier transform as a unitary change to the character basis — ℤ₂^n from unit 13 and ℤ_N as two instances of one theorem. On ℤ_2^n the transform of a basis state is a product state, proved, and that product formula is the circuit: n Hadamards and n(n−1)/2 controlled phases, against O(n2^n) for the classical FFT on the same vector — with the caveat, stated loudly, that you cannot read the output vector.
units.tools: The approximate QFT: dropping rotations below 2π/2^m costs at most O(n2^−m), so O(n log n) gates suffice (Coppersmith 1994, proved). Phase estimation: given U and an eigenvector, t ancillas give the eigenphase to the nearest t-bit fraction with probability at least 4/π² ≈ 0.405, and n + ⌈log₂(2 + 1/2ε)⌉ ancillas give n bits with probability 1 − ε, both proved.
units.problems: The slides draw the QFT circuit for three qubits and the phase-estimation peak. The sheet: for eigenphase 1/3 with three ancillas, compute the full outcome distribution — the nearest fraction 3/8 appears with probability 0.688; derive the product formula; show the approximate-QFT error bound.
units.checkpoint: You derive the QFT circuit from the product formula, prove the 4/π² bound, and compute the three-ancilla distribution for phase 1/3.

units.title: Shor: factoring is order finding, and order finding is phase estimation
units.theory: The reduction, proved: for odd N with at least two distinct prime factors, a random a coprime to N has even order r with a^r/2 ≢ −1 with probability at least ½ — a CRT argument — and then gcd(a^r/2 ± 1, N) splits N. Order finding as phase estimation on x ↦ ax mod N, whose eigenphases are s/r. Modular exponentiation by repeated squaring as a reversible circuit of O(n³) gates. The same machinery solves discrete logarithms, which is why elliptic-curve cryptography falls with RSA.
units.tools: Continued fractions, and Legendre's theorem, proved: if |x − p/q| < 1/(2q²) then p/q is a convergent of x. Recovering r when gcd(s, r) > 1, by repetition and least common multiples. The hidden subgroup problem as the frame for Simon, Shor and discrete log; the abelian case solved, the dihedral and symmetric cases — lattices and graph isomorphism — stated as open.
units.problems: The slides factor 15 with a = 7: order 4, 7² = 49 ≡ 4, gcd(3, 15) = 3 and gcd(5, 15) = 5. The sheet does 21 in full with a = 2 and nine counting qubits (21² ≤ 2⁹ < 2 · 21²): the outcome distribution peaks at 0, 85, 171, 256, 341 and 427; 427/512 has convergent 5/6, giving r = 6, then 2³ = 8 and gcd(7, 21), gcd(9, 21) give 7 and 3. Also: compute the probability that one run yields r = 6 directly (0.308), and explain what the other peaks give.
units.checkpoint: You prove the order-finding reduction and Legendre's theorem, and factor 21 by hand from the measured distribution, including the runs that fail and why.

units.title: Grover: search as a rotation in a plane
units.theory: The whole algorithm lives in the two-dimensional plane spanned by the uniform superposition and the marked states, and one Grover iteration — two reflections — is a rotation by 2θ with sin θ = √(M/N), proved and drawn. Hence ≈ (π/4)√(N/M) iterations, success probability at least 1 − M/N, and the overshoot when you iterate too long. Amplitude amplification: the same rotation boosts any algorithm with success probability p to near certainty in O(1/√p) runs.
units.tools: Unknown M: exponentially growing random iteration counts reach expected O(√(N/M)) (Boyer–Brassard–Høyer–Tapp 1998, proved). Quantum counting as phase estimation on the Grover rotation, joining this unit to unit 15. Applied to key search: AES-128 in about 2⁶⁴ sequential iterations, which is why the response is longer keys rather than new ciphers — and why the sequential depth, not the count, is the real obstacle.
units.problems: The sheet: for N = 2²⁰ and one marked item, find the optimal iteration count (804) and its success probability (above 0.999 999 7); find N for which exactly one iteration succeeds with certainty (N = 4); prove the overshoot is periodic.
units.checkpoint: You prove the two-reflection rotation picture, and produce 804 iterations and the success probability for a million-item search.

units.title: Lower bounds: what quantum computers provably cannot do
units.theory: The hybrid argument (Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani 1997), proved: any algorithm finding a marked item among N needs Ω(√N) queries, so Grover is optimal and brute-force search over NP witnesses gains a square root and no more. Relative to a random oracle, NP ⊄ BQP. The polynomial method (Beals–Buhrman–Cleve–Mosca–de Wolf 1998), proved: after T queries every acceptance probability is a polynomial of degree at most 2T in the input bits.
units.tools: Symmetrisation (Minsky–Papert), proved, reducing symmetric functions to univariate polynomials. Approximate degree of OR at Θ(√N) (Nisan–Szegedy, Paturi, cited). For total functions, deterministic query complexity is at most a fourth power of quantum (Aaronson–Ben-David–Kothari–Rao–Tal 2021, cited): exponential speedups need a promise — which is exactly what Simon and Shor have and search does not.
units.problems: The slides draw the hybrid argument as a sum of small perturbations. The sheet: show parity of N bits takes exactly N/2 quantum queries — the upper bound from Deutsch's algorithm on pairs, the lower bound from degree; prove the BBBV bound with explicit constants.
units.checkpoint: You prove Ω(√N) for search by the hybrid argument and exactly N/2 for parity by the polynomial method.

units.title: Hamiltonian simulation: Feynman's reason, made into an algorithm
units.theory: Feynman's 1981 argument: simulating n spins classically tracks 2^n amplitudes, so build the simulator out of spins. Local Hamiltonians as the physically relevant class; the transverse-field Ising chain as the running example. Lie–Trotter: for non-commuting A, B, (e^−iAt/ne^−iBt/n)^n approaches e^−i(A+B)t with error at most ‖[A, B]‖t²/2n, proved; Strang's symmetric splitting to second order. Phase estimation on the simulated evolution reads off energies.
units.tools: Commutator scaling of Trotter error (Childs–Su–Tran–Wiebe–Zhu 2021, cited). Gate counts for a k-local Hamiltonian on n qubits. Qubitisation and quantum signal processing named as the optimal methods. Branch 20 is the other side of the coin: dynamics is easy for a quantum computer, ground energies are not. (Mechanics to Relativity unit 14 is the classical picture: a Hamiltonian generates a flow, and splitting it is how symplectic integrators work.)
units.problems: The sheet: for H = X + Z on one qubit at t = 1, compute the actual first-order Trotter error at n = 10 (0.070) against the bound ‖[X, Z]‖/2n = 0.1; count the Trotter steps for an Ising chain to given accuracy.
units.checkpoint: You prove the first-order Trotter bound and size a Trotterised Ising simulation for a target accuracy.

units.title: QMA and the local Hamiltonian problem: Cook–Levin, quantum
units.theory: Merlin sends a quantum proof; Arthur checks it with a BQP circuit. QMA defined with completeness ⅔ and soundness ⅓ — and amplification is no longer free, because the witness cannot be copied. Parallel repetition on a product of witnesses works and entangled cheating witnesses do not help, proved; Marriott–Watrous in-place amplification stated (cited). The k-local Hamiltonian problem: given H = ΣH_j, each term on k qubits with ‖H_j‖ ≤ 1, decide whether the ground energy is at most a or at least b, with b − a ≥ 1/poly. The classical case first: a k-SAT formula is a diagonal k-local Hamiltonian counting violated clauses, so the problem is NP-hard before anything quantum happens. Unit 19 showed a quantum computer simulates dynamics efficiently; this unit shows that finding a ground state — what a chemist most wants — is hard in the worst case even for one.
units.tools: Membership: Arthur measures one randomly chosen term on Merlin's state, proved. Hardness, Kitaev's theorem that 5-local Hamiltonian is QMA-complete, proved: the Feynman–Kitaev history state Σ_t U_t⋯U₁|ξ⟩ ⊗ |t⟩ with a unary clock; the input, output, clock and propagation terms; the propagation term unitarily equivalent to the Laplacian of a path, with spectral gap 1 − cos(π/(T+1)) = Θ(1/T²), proved; soundness from the geometric lemma on the angle between two null spaces, proved. 2-local completeness (Kempe–Kitaev–Regev 2006) and one-dimensional chains (Aharonov–Gottesman–Irani–Kempe 2009) cited; the quantum PCP conjecture and the NLTS theorem (Anshu–Breuckmann–Nirkhe 2023) named.
units.problems: The slides set Cook–Levin's tableau beside the history state, row for clock step: a classical tableau's consistency is checked locally, a history state's is enforced by energy penalties, and the price is a promise gap of 1/poly instead of a constant. The sheet: write a 3-SAT instance as a diagonal 3-local Hamiltonian and read off its ground energy; build the propagation term for a nine-gate circuit and find its gap, 1 − cos(π/10) ≈ 0.0489; show the history state of an accepting computation has zero propagation energy; prove membership in QMA.
units.checkpoint: You prove the local Hamiltonian problem is in QMA, construct the Feynman–Kitaev Hamiltonian for a given circuit, and prove its propagation term has gap 1 − cos(π/(T+1)) — 0.0489 for nine gates.

units.title: Open systems: measurements and channels in full generality
units.theory: A qubit in a real device leaks energy to its surroundings and loses phase; neither is unitary on the qubit alone. POVMs and Naimark's dilation, proved: every generalised measurement is a projective one on a larger space. Channels as completely positive trace-preserving maps, and why positivity alone is not enough: the transpose is positive and not completely positive, proved with |Φ⁺⟩. Choi's theorem, the Kraus representation and Stinespring dilation, proved in finite dimension.
units.tools: The standard noise models — bit flip, phase flip, depolarising, amplitude damping (T₁), dephasing (T₂) — as Kraus families, and T₂ ≤ 2T₁ within this model, proved. Trace distance and fidelity; trace distance contracts under every channel, proved, so no processing can make two states more distinguishable.
units.problems: The sheet pays unit 05's debt: unambiguous discrimination of |0⟩ and |+⟩ by a three-outcome POVM succeeds with probability 1 − 1/√2 ≈ 0.293, and Naimark turns it into a projective measurement on a qutrit. Also: derive amplitude damping from a Stinespring dilation; find two Kraus families for the same channel and the unitary relating them.
units.checkpoint: You prove Choi's theorem and that the transpose is not completely positive, and derive T₂ ≤ 2T₁.

units.title: The first quantum codes, and the conditions that say when any code works
units.theory: Three reasons quantum error correction looks impossible — no-cloning forbids repetition, errors are continuous, measurement destroys the state — and the three-qubit bit-flip code answering all three: encode by entangling, measure only parities, correct. The phase-flip code by Hadamard conjugation, and Shor's nine-qubit code (1995) as the two composed. Classical linear codes over 𝔽₂ as far as the Hamming [7, 4, 3] code, because unit 23 needs it.
units.tools: The Knill–Laflamme conditions, proved necessary and sufficient: P E_i†E_j P = α_ijP. The discretisation of errors, proved from linearity: a code correcting X, Y, Z on any one qubit corrects every single-qubit channel. Distance, and degenerate codes.
units.problems: The slides draw the syndrome circuit for the bit-flip code. The sheet: logical failure of the bit-flip code under independent flips is 3p² − 2p³, below p exactly when p < ½, and 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ at p = 10⁻³; verify Knill–Laflamme for Shor's code; show the bit-flip code fails against a single phase flip.
units.checkpoint: You prove Knill–Laflamme in both directions and the discretisation of errors, and verify Shor's code corrects an arbitrary single-qubit error.

units.title: Stabilisers: codes as abelian groups, and the circuits a classical computer can run
units.theory: A code as the joint +1 eigenspace of an abelian subgroup of the Pauli group not containing −I; dimension 2^n−k for n − k independent generators, proved. Syndromes as anticommutation patterns, logical operators as the normaliser modulo the stabiliser, distance as the lightest nontrivial logical. The CSS construction from nested classical codes, proved, and Steane's [[7, 1, 3]] from Hamming. The five-qubit code as the smallest correcting one error.
units.tools: The binary symplectic representation of Paulis, turning stabiliser questions into linear algebra over 𝔽₂. The Gottesman–Knill theorem, proved: Clifford circuits on stabiliser states with Pauli measurements are simulable classically in polynomial time — so entanglement alone does not make a computation hard, and the non-Clifford T gate is where the power is. The quantum Hamming bound for non-degenerate codes.
units.problems: The sheet: derive Steane's stabilisers from Hamming's parity checks; find its logical X and Z; show transversal H implements logical H; check the five-qubit code meets the quantum Hamming bound with equality, 2⁵ = (1 + 3 · 5) · 2.
units.checkpoint: You prove Gottesman–Knill and the CSS construction, and build Steane's code with its logical operators from the Hamming code.

units.title: Fault tolerance: the threshold theorem, magic states, and the surface code
units.theory: Correction circuits are themselves faulty, and a CNOT copies an X error forward and a Z error back — drawn. Fault-tolerant gadgets and transversal gates. The threshold theorem for concatenated codes, proved in a simplified model: if one level maps p ↦ cp², then k levels give (cp)^2k/c, doubly exponential suppression below p = 1/c; the full theorem cited (Aharonov–Ben-Or, Kitaev, Knill–Laflamme–Zurek).
units.tools: Eastin–Knill, stated: no code has a transversal universal gate set. So T is injected: gate teleportation with the magic state T|+⟩, proved, and 15-to-1 distillation taking error p to 35p³ (Bravyi–Kitaev 2005, cited). The surface code on its lattice, drawn: distance d, about 2d² − 1 physical qubits, logical error roughly A(p/p_th)^(d+1)/2 with a threshold near 1 per cent. Google's 2024 below-threshold experiment, distance 3 to 7, cited with its suppression factor.
units.problems: The sheet: with p = 10⁻³, p_th = 10⁻² and A = 0.1, find the distance for logical error at most 10⁻¹² per cycle (d = 21) and the physical cost per logical qubit (881); find the levels of concatenation that do the same job; prove the magic-state teleportation circuit.
units.checkpoint: You prove the concatenated threshold in the simplified model, and size a surface-code logical qubit for a stated physical error rate and target.

units.title: The physical qubit: driving a transmon, and the third level that will not stay empty
units.theory: Every earlier unit treats a qubit as ℂ²; a superconducting qubit is not one. It is a weakly anharmonic oscillator — levels at 0, ω and 2ω + α, with ω/2π near 5 GHz and anharmonicity α/2π near −250 MHz — and the qubit is its lowest two levels, with nothing but α keeping the third away. The ladder is taken as given, with its origin cited (Koch et al. 2007): deriving it means quantising a circuit, which needs infinite-dimensional quantum mechanics (open question 5). Everything after it is finite-dimensional. A microwave drive in the lab frame; the rotating frame as a time-dependent change of basis, with the transformed Hamiltonian derived; the rotating-wave approximation, stated with its condition; Rabi oscillation and the π-pulse as unit 02's rotations made physical.
units.tools: Time-dependent Hamiltonians, evolved as a product of short-time exponentials with the error of the piecewise-constant approximation bounded. The truncated ladder operator, whose |1⟩ → |2⟩ element is √2: the drive couples to the leakage transition more strongly than to the qubit one, detuned only by α. DRAG (Motzoi–Gambetta–Rebentrost–Wilhelm 2009): a second quadrature proportional to the envelope's derivative over α, derived to first order. The drive also shifts the qubit's own frequency — an AC Stark shift — repaired by a detuning proportional to Ω²/α; the correction that minimises leakage is not the one that minimises gate error (Gambetta et al. 2011, cited). Unit 21's amplitude damping as a gate error: average infidelity t/3T₁ for short gates, proved.
units.problems: The slides drive a 10 ns Gaussian π-pulse into a three-level transmon at α/2π = −250 MHz and plot the populations through the pulse: 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ ends in |2⟩; at 4 ns, a quarter of the population leaks. The sheet: derive the rotating-frame Hamiltonian; add the derivative correction and watch leakage fall to about 4 × 10⁻⁶ while the rotation still misses |1⟩ by 2.6 per cent; find the detuning that repairs most of that; then compare with decoherence — a 20 ns gate at T₁ = 100 µs has average infidelity 6.7 × 10⁻⁵, so on these numbers control, not T₁, sets the floor. (Mechanics to Relativity's unit 21b solves the harmonic oscillator by ladder operators — the ladder this unit's transmon starts from.)
units.checkpoint: You derive the rotating-frame Hamiltonian under the rotating-wave approximation, compute the 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ leakage of a 10 ns Gaussian π-pulse and what the derivative correction does to it, and say which of leakage, Stark shift and T₁ dominates the gate error.

units.title: Hardware and the near term: what exists, what it has shown, and what it has not
units.theory: DiVincenzo's criteria as the lens, applied to platforms rather than vendors: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons — each with what limits its T₁, its gate fidelity and its connectivity; unit 25 took one apart in full, and here it is one of four. Why superconducting qubits need a dilution refrigerator, as a Boltzmann factor. Random-circuit sampling: the 2019 supremacy claim, the classical simulations that later narrowed it, and what the episode says about moving baselines. Variational algorithms, with QAOA on Max-Cut as the example — the sister course's unit 25 is the classical side of the comparison.
units.tools: QAOA at depth one on triangle-free 3-regular graphs, analysed exactly: expected cut fraction ½ + 1/(3√3) ≈ 0.6925, against Goemans–Williamson's 0.878. Dequantisation (Tang 2018, cited): a claimed exponential speedup for recommendation systems that turned out to be a better classical algorithm waiting to be found.
units.problems: The sheet: thermal excited-state population of a 5 GHz qubit — hf/k_BT ≈ 12 at 20 mK, so about 6 × 10⁻⁶, and 0.06 at 4 K, so nearly maximally mixed; derive the depth-one QAOA edge expectation; set a claimed advantage against the classical baseline it should have been compared to.
units.checkpoint: You compute the thermal populations at 20 mK and 4 K, derive the 0.6925 QAOA ratio, and state for one published advantage claim exactly which classical algorithm it was measured against.
